content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper performs an analysis about the (binary) entropy of the features of a k-contrastive distinguisher model to understand the impact of low/high entropy features on the generalization to other domains. The conclusion is that masking can be beneficial in some contexts, especially when filtering the most certain features, while uncertain features tend to generalise better and carry more information.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The conclusions drawn are reasonable and quite intuitive
- The paper is mostly clear (although presentation quality can be improved, see comments), the diagram is helpful

Weaknesses:
- Q1: The result is not particularly surprising. Intuitively, I would expect high confidence features in this setup to be less robust given neural networks tend to rely on simple discriminative but spurious features and to learn shortcuts to solve tasks. And it is commonly believed that these shortcuts prevent them from generalising under distribution shift. Did the authors have a look at the spurious-correlation literature  (e.g. consider doing experiments where spurious features are known and controlled like in Waterbirds and CelebA [1] (yes, same reference), ImageNet-9 [2], Colored-MNIST [3] or the MNIST-CIFAR simplicity bias experiment [4])? I feel like the insights of the paper would be much deeper if it would be possible to associate high/low entropy features to spurious features in controlled setups. Obviously these are classification datasets, but you could creatively use them for image identification to show that high-entropy features are more associated with invariant variables (e.g. foreground object, complex features etc.) and low-entropy features are more associated with spurious ones (e.g. background, colour, simple features). This would nicely connect your work with existing literature.  Analysing these things could also very likely help you to understand why you observe an increase in accuracy on in-distribution data when masking. I conjecture it is due to removing spurious but simple features that do not even generalise to the in-distribution test set (that's also why I'm not particularly surprised by the phenomenon you observe). Could you please perform some controlled experiments to check it?
- Q2: It is unclear how practical and general the conclusions drawn in this paper can be. This setup looks heavily tuned to perform these types of analyses rather than analysing actual architectures/methodologies in use. It might be my little knowledge of object identification literature, but I don't recall this type of architecture being used commonly. Could the authors either provide references about recent papers using very similar setups or show that this setup can produce at least comparable performance to recent SOTA methodologies? 
- Q3: Could the authors take a practically used model and show that their conclusions somehow generalise (even applying a few simplifications to these models to make the frameworks compatible)?

Additional comments:
- Sometimes the order in which figures are referenced in the text does not reflect their order in the paper. 
- the plots look a bit dirty
- The structure and the exposition can be improved. 

[1] https://github.com/kohpangwei/group_DRO
[2] https://github.com/MadryLab/backgrounds_challenge
[3] https://github.com/reiinakano/invariant-risk-minimization
[4] https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.07710
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is mostly clear, but the quality of the presentation can be improved. The quality is acceptable, although the applicability of the conclusions is questionable. The results are not particularly surprising to me, but with the suggested experiments I feel like the paper could connect nicely to the literature and become more appealing. The work seems to be relatively easy to reproduce.
content.summary_of_the_review: The intuition of the paper is interesting, but I feel like the authors should try to relate better to the existing literature both to improve the applicability of their insights or to improve our understanding of SOTA identification techniques, and to better understand how their contribution can be contextualised in the current theoretical discussion about distribution-shift generalization and its relationship with spurious variables learning. I would encourage them to perform a further effort in these directions as their submission would very likely benefit from it, although this might require an extensive rewriting of some parts of the paper.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper designs experiments to test the relevance of low vs high entropy features in the context of OOD failure.

The authors do this in a CIFAR-10-trained setup where they first learn a representation using a contrastive-learning technique. They motivate the use of a contrastive objective because it is most compatible with having a (differentiable) binary hidden representation on which entropy can be computed easily (when compared to other techniques like autoencoders etc.,). 

The authors then consider masking either random bits in the representation, or the bits with the top or the bottommost entropy. The main observations are that masking least entropy can leads to an increase in in-distribution accuracy and out-of-distribution accuracy.

The experiments are on CIFAR-10 trained for 16 different hyperparameter configurations (4 values of k, the number of competing examples in contrastive-learning task, and r the length of the binary representation). For OOD, the authors test on essentially 3 different target distributions, MNIST, Plant Village, Colorectal Histology.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths
===

1. Understanding which features are useful vs hurtful for OOD is an important scientific question that can lead to principled solutions.
2. The idea of examining entropy of features in this context is novel.
3. The idea of using a binarizing layer (with a contrastive task) in order to compute entropy is neat.
4. It is indeed interesting that somehow removing the low entropy bits results in a substantial increase in OOD accuracy.

Weaknessess
===

1. The paper restricts itself to one source distribution (CIFAR-10) and three target distributions effectively. This is unfortunately overly restrictive for an empirical paper as it's not clear how well these insights generalize. 

2. Overall the result requires more depth to be publishable. The one key takeaway for me was the positive effect of removing the bottom entropy bits in a specific setting. But there are many ways to dig further into this:
- For example, the paper could have provided hypotheses/theories for when and why the low entropy bits are worth masking and verify/refute those hypotheses in practice.
- The paper could have designed (synthetic) settings where it is possible to identify which bits corresponds to which features, to visualize what features actually correspond to low entropy features.

- On this note, the paper spends much of its time analyzing the effect of "k" which is the number of distractors in the contrastive task. This to me is not a significant/fundamental quantity, and is more of an artifact of the contrastive learning task. While it is good that the paper analyzes the effect of this carefully, this should have been a small part of more important analyses.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There were multiple aspects of the paper where I'd like a clarification:

1. I'd like to understand why a classification task is unsuited for learning a representation here. My understanding is that the even with the contrastive task, for each target distribution a new head must be learned? So why not do the same for a classification task?

2. Perhaps my above question arises from the lack of clarity in how exactly the OOD task is trained on and evaluated.

3. It's not clear to me if masking happens before or after OOD training. 

4. The motivating example in the introduction maybe a bit confusing. Often, features such as the "sky" is typically thought of as a bad feature for out-of-distribution tasks, as it may be a spurious correlation (see for example, https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.02893, and other follow-up works) -- this is the opposite of what is suggested in the intro. Consequently, this line of work argues that more detailed features such as the shape of an object on the other hand, could actually be more useful for OOD tasks. 

Also, in contrast to what is suggested in the intro, one might also suspect that overall the sky pixels together have much lower entropy than the pixels corresponding to the object in the middle.

In summary, there are two confusing aspects in this motivating example that hints at some fundamental questions:
 (a) it's not clear how to connect simple vs detailed features to high vs low entropy of a single bit
 (b) it's not clear if the connection between low entropy and OOD improvement is an artifact of certain settings that will no longer hold in other settings.

#### Minor

1. I'd suggest labeling the y axis everywhere.
2. Sec 3.1 could be better written as it was not immediately clear _why_ we were looking at the distribution of entropies.
content.summary_of_the_review: The key result showing that masking low entropy results in higher OOD accuracy is very interesting and has the potential to be the core of a solid paper. However the current paper lacks the depth and breadth required to be publishable due to restrictive experiment settings and limited insights.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper study the relationship between the entropy of intermediate representations and the models’ robustness to distributional shift. Especially, the authors adopt a set of different masking strategies, which removes low-entropy bits, high-entropy bits, and random bits. Accordingly, the authors find that 1) the removal of bits via any strategy leads to an increase in performance, when masking out a relatively low proportion of bits; 2) the removal of low-entropy bits can notably benefit OOD performance; and 3) top-entropy masking disproportionately harms performance for both ID and OOD cases.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

The authors demonstrate that the removal of low-entropy representations via the masking of learned discrete bits can notably improve OOD performance, which is different from much of previous works that consider domain randomization and auxiliary loss functions. The paper is the pioneer in studying the relation between the entropy and the OOD generalization. So, the novelty of this paper is ok for me. 

The authors conduct extensive experiments on a set of different datasets (CIFAR, Colorectal Histology, MNIST, Plant Village, etc) with a set of different masking strategies (masked bottom entropy, masked top entropy, and random mask). They test both the ID and OOD performance. Then they have three findings associated with the relation between entropy and OOD generalization. So, I think the experimental results are relatively convincing. 

Cons: 

There are other methods in OOD generalization with model masking, e.g., [1]. So, a natural question is what the difference between the proposed method and the existing works is. Also, another important question is why the proposed method can be superior to the existing works. More discussions and more experiments in comparison may require. 

[1] Dinghuai Zhang, et al. Can subnetwork structure be the key to OOD generalization? ICML’21. 

It seems that the proposed method is strongly bound with a particular choice of the model. Therefore, I am a bit concern about if the conclusion is applicable to other choices of the models. 

The authors mainly verify their three findings in the experimental parts. However, I think there lack of sufficient studies in comparing the proposed methods over the advanced counterparts. To me, I think verifying the superiority (or the effectiveness) of a new method over existing methods can be important, which can make the proposal more contributive.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty of this paper is not enough for ICLR. Please refer to Cons in Strength And Weaknesses. Clarity and reproducibility are good to me.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper seeks to study factors governing out-of-distribution generalization for a particular unsupervised contrastive learning task on images. The idea is to create a model which encodes an image into a discrete $r$-dimensional latent binary vector, which is then appended to a set of representations corresponding to $k$ other images in some random order, one of which is the original image. These are fed into a Transformer which then outputs a single index which is supposed to correspond to the index of the original image. This model is trained on CIFAR-10, and the paper then studies the impact of various masks on the $r$-dimensional discrete binary vector, which are organized by their impact on the highest or lowest entropy bits in the representation. In particular, for performance in-distribution, the paper empirically finds that removing high-entropy bits is most damaging to performance, the small $k$ task has similar performance regardless of the entropy-related filter used to mask, and for small $k$, masking can even improve performance. For out-of-distribution, which in this paper is defined as performance on the Plant Village dataset, the Colorectal Histology dataset, and MNIST (for this contrastive learning task), it turns out that masking the lowest entropy bits or random bits leads to the best performance.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
* Strengths: The paper proposes an interesting metric by which to index OOD performance of machine learning models, namely the entropy of a binary latent variable.



* Weaknesses: 
    * Out-of-distribution is not well-defined in the paper -- there is a heuristic thrust at the kind of out-of-distribution performance the results are supposed to apply to, but it is rather imprecise. I would recommend coming up with a more concrete definition of "out-of-distribution" -- as is, it is very unclear to what kind of other out of distribution datasets the results of the paper would apply to.
    * The choice of out of distribution datasets seems somewhat arbitrary (outside of the correction for datasets which have similar performance to the "in-distribution" dataset. It is also somewhat odd to me that the method has the same performance on CIFAR100 after being trained on CIFAR10, and it is even more surprising that this is true for the Stanford Shopping dataset.
    * The model studied seems ad-hoc and arbitrary -- it is not clear why we should care about the impact of the binary latent variables for this particular task and architecture, and it is not clear how the results should generalize to other settings (models and datasets). However, the idea of investigating the impact of the entropy of a binarized version of a latent variable does seem interesting and worthy of further investigation. What I would suggest is to instead find a way to take $\textit{existing}$ models that have been trained, and find a way to do a similar test on the weights of the already trained model, rather than re-training for a specific unsupervised contrastive learning task. If the ideas can be formulated in terms of a diagnostic that can be applied to any model, that would be far more interesting from an understanding perspective, while also being applicable as a diagnostic test. 
    * The variance of the results was incredibly high -- see Table 2 for instance, the error bars are many factors larger than the mean values, and it is unclear whether the trend is positive or negative. I also found the explanation of Figure 8 unclear and unconvincing. Relatedly, Figure 4 and 5 are also not very convincing and it's not clear that a linear regression here is a particularly useful way to interpret this data - at least it should be plotted with the uncertainty estimate range, otherwise it's misleading.
    * It's also not clear why an unsupervised task setting was necessary (re: Section 2.4) -- there are several "alternate ImageNet" datasets available that have been created to test OOD on ImageNet (see for instance https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10811). 
    * Additionally, the relation of the proposed ideas to variational inference (e.g. the Bits Back method mentioned in Related Work) and Variational Autoencoders should be further expounded upon.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Clarity: The paper was fairly clear, but some sections could benefit from re-writing: 
   * The introduction needs a definition of what out-of-distribution actually means -- in fact it is never precisely stated anywhere what out of distribution means in the context of this paper (comparison to some specific vision datasets after training on CIFAR10). 
   * The language describing Fig. 2 and the communication channel on pg. 2 is confusing: is the purple rectangle in Fig. 2 $r$-dimensional? It looks larger in the picture, which is confusing.
   * The description of the method applied from Taori et. al. on pg. 7 is hard to parse and not complete, for instance how do you get the CIFAR10 models with differing accuracies?


* Quality: The paper feels unready for publication.


* Novelty: Some of the ideas in the paper seem novel and interesting, and I would encourage the authors to continue to develop their ideas perhaps along a slightly different line. I did find this work which seems related after a quick search: https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3491243. 

This p
* Reproducibility: The work seems somewhat reproducible in terms of implementability of the experiments, though I would have concerns about the variances of the results -- it seems plausible that one might reach different conclusions.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, I think there is a potentially interesting idea present in the paper, but I would recommend different experiments and more rigor in defining the problem actually being studied. In particular, the study is both too limited to make the conclusions the paper wants to make in the abstract and introduction, and the results are too high-variance to make these conclusions as well. Thus I must recommend rejection, but I encourage the authors to take another stab at re-working some of the experiments and ideas so they may apply more generally -- I think it would be particularly interesting to find a way to apply some of the ideas to frozen, already-trained networks -- maybe one can do a similar contrastive experiment without performing additional training? What would be crucial to do is develop an approach to measuring the entropy of latent variables (perhaps by discretizing intermediate layers of the frozen network whose OOD performance (to be defined more carefully)) of the network in a more general manner. After a brief search, I did not find papers applying this specific idea, but it seems likely to me that there are some papers out there which have at least looked at this kind of measure before, so I would recommend doing a thorough literature review. Separately, regarding the question the authors ask on why removing bits in the training distribution would help increase performance: perhaps this recent paper https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05739 is relevant for further investigation -- if misleading data is present in the dataset (in both train and test), perhaps some of the bits are encoding this (note that simply checking that overfitting is not happening would not rule this hypothesis out).  This paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.08220) also seems related and of interest.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
